The wording here is not fully clear. At first it seems to refer to the power to act, but its ending seems to refer to the capacity to be affected, as the phrase “the actual and the possible would be together” suggests. The point holds either way. A particular action comes from outside causes; it does not come from the power alone. Power and action also come in degrees. If this is power to act, it is at a stronger level than the action it produces. If it is the capacity to be affected, the relation is reversed: the actual change is stronger than the capacity to receive it. The note promises to explain this further.

You might object that this argument does not work. It discusses the power to act, not the capacity to be affected, and there is no problem with the power to act existing at the same time as the result it produces. The real problem would be for a thing's readiness to remain once what it was ready for had become actual. The reply is that if the power to act on one particular individual remained after that individual came into being, then, on the recipient's side, the capacity to be affected would remain alongside the actual result. The same thing would then be both still only possible and already actual, which is impossible. This confirms the point: power directed at one particular individual ends when that individual exists, while power directed at an unspecified individual of the same kind remains.

Even more surprising, many later writers, including al-Fakhrī, accepted this explanation and tried to reconcile the two views. They said that those who required power to be present with the action meant a power with all the conditions needed to produce the effect; those who said power came before the action meant a power still missing some of those conditions. The commentator says this confuses two meanings. An animal's ability is a power that comes with the possibility of acting or not acting. That possibility cannot exist at the same time as its full realization. A power with every condition in place is power in another sense.

As Chapter 1 explained, much of the earlier discussion comes from the Imam's Al-Mabāḥith al-Mashriqiyya. The thinkers meant that power accompanies an action when power means that the action can proceed. But the Imam explained their claim in terms of the complete power to cause the action: the acting cause together with all the other things a complete cause needs. His wording shows this. He therefore shifts between two meanings of power.

The conditional “if He wills, He acts” can be made up of two necessary statements. God is necessary in Himself and in every respect, both in what He is and in what He does. These two meanings of power do not imply each other, contrary to what some theologians say. The possibility of acting or not acting does not apply to God's power. But the statement “if He wills, He acts” does. A conditional statement does not always mean that the outcome could be otherwise. It can be true when both parts are necessary, or even when both are impossible.

An agent may have no motive at all, like someone who acts at random, according to theologians. Philosophers say that even such a person has some aim. Or an agent may have no added motive, which is the usual meaning of “without a motive.” This is how philosophers describe the Necessary Being.

The difference is that a person acting at random acts from an arbitrary will, while someone acting from a motive acts from a considered will. In either case, the will and motive may be part of the agent's own nature or something added to it.

In our earlier discussion of cause and effect, we questioned whether there is really a separate kind of agent whose action comes from its knowledge. It may instead belong with the kind whose own self-knowledge is enough to bring about its action. But an agent whose action is a self-disclosure, mentioned later in the discussion of God, may be a separate kind.

Here the author criticizes the view held by Aristotle’s followers that God's knowledge consists of forms or images of things, which then cause them to appear. If God is the Light of Lights, and light is what makes things visible, the true light does not need images to know things. Its light itself reveals them and reaches into their depths.
This points to another kind of agent: one whose action is a self-disclosure. Earlier notes explain this kind.

Our earlier discussion of cause and effect gave a fuller account and showed that the division into “free” and “compelled” is a familiar way of speaking, not a division into two completely separate kinds. The author's use of “free” and “compelled” here depends on what those words mean. An action is free in the fullest sense when it comes from an agent that knows what it is doing and can cause it on its own. It is compelled in this sense when the agent does not know what it is doing, or knows but cannot act on its own. This differs from the other meaning of “free”: that an agent can act if it wills and refrain if it does not. The author calls all created agents subject to God, whether they choose or are forced, because God alone acts entirely on His own. Created agents can be both free and dependent only in the first sense of these words. In the second sense, freedom and compulsion are opposites.

Avicenna says that powers linked to reason and imagination can grasp opposite things: one power can know what is human and what is not human, and imagine pleasure and pain. The author changes Avicenna's line of argument because Avicenna treats perception as something received, while he treats it as an activity. He says that sensing and imagining bring their objects about, and that understanding is the mind's own activity. Philosophers also speak of a “simple intellect”: a settled kind of knowledge already present in an intellect fully at work, which does not need to learn anything new.
The phrase should be “source of change,” not “source of motion.” This wider wording includes coming into being and passing away, which these philosophers consider instantaneous.

We have already explained that causes work within nature, between nature and what lies beyond it, and among higher things. Those who study nature call nature the cause of change in the natural world; those who study existence more broadly use “source of existence” in a wider sense. So Mulla Sadra's claim that God is most deserving of the name “agent” does not mean that nature cannot cause change or that other causes cannot bring particular things into being.

God gives existence to matter and to its readiness; He brings them out of nonexistence. A natural cause, by contrast, only changes matter after God has brought it into being and after it is ready. Once it is ready, its forms come from the world beyond matter, from God, who gives forms. This is one meaning of the teaching of “a middle way between two extremes” about God's power over all things: God is the cause of everything because He gives existence without limit. Other things are causes as sources of movement and change, not as sources of existence. Even motion itself lies between pure possibility and complete actuality.

The actions and words used in prayer can lead to calm and trust in God, or to worshipping other things alongside Him. Neither outcome is a bodily movement. The note shows three differences between a skill learned through practice and action that comes from habit: skill uses outside materials and tools; the person aims to gain the skill, while a habit may arise as a side effect; and the learned skill gives shape to the actions it produces, which are of the same kind as the skill. Habit differs in all three ways.

This does not mean that action from habit and action from skill are the same thing, or that there are no real differences between them. Both come from a lasting quality of the soul; they differ in what they aim at and how they begin.

The meaning of chance has already been explained. The author may have written these and similar passages before he put the discussion in its present order. He first planned to discuss power and action before cause and effect, but arranged them the other way around in the final version.

The author made this point just before and repeats it here to address two familiar claims based on the idea that a thing needs a cause because it began to exist. That starting idea has no good basis. The two claims are that an effect must have been nonexistent for some time, and that it no longer needs its cause once it exists. These claims make sense only for actions that unfold over time, such as motion, time, or nature working through bodies. Such an action exists as a sequence of parts. Each part comes after a period when it did not exist, and each part can itself be divided further. It does not need a cause to continue, because it does not last as a single thing. Even so, while natural powers and processes bring it about, it is also an act of God, who encompasses all.

By nonexistence, the theologians mean that something did not exist at an earlier time. If they meant nonexistence in a broader sense, an eternal action could still exist. This is why they also claimed that time is only imagined or comes from God's own being. They wanted to avoid two problems: time itself would count as an eternal action, or every time would need an earlier time without end. But if time is only imagined, the whole discussion falls apart and their condition makes no sense. If time comes from God's own being, then God Himself would have to change. They may reply that something can come from a source and still differ from it. But that would let ideas differ from the real things they describe, so our ideas would not need to match reality.
This also shows that the soul itself is not the body's temperament.

“In the broadest sense” includes transition from nonexistence to existence and from possibility to necessity. It also includes both sudden and gradual transitions from potentiality to actuality. One might object that coming from nonexistence to existence, as in the case of intellects, is motion only figuratively, and that a sudden transition, as in coming to be or passing away, requires a thing to belong to a particular natural kind. The reply is that even if such a transition is called motion figuratively, and coming to be or passing away requires a natural kind because it belongs to a natural body, substantial motion—the flow of nature itself—is not an attribute of a body but one of its principles. Since nature is flowing existence, it is prior to the body. Its natural kind follows from bodyhood itself, not from a later classification.

“In the broadest sense” is explained below as any transition from potentiality to actuality, sudden or gradual, and the lack of such a transition in something that can undergo one. The author says these apply to things before they are classified as natural or mathematical kinds. But such transitions occur only in things made up of potentiality and actuality, either in themselves or through a subject: bodily substances. That is already a natural classification. Moreover, many of the rules discussed in this and the following stages apply only to motion in the narrower sense, as a feature of natural bodies. Broadening the word to include coming to be, passing away, and other changes does not help. It is better to divide existing things into stable and flowing things, alongside the division into actual and potential. One can then discuss features shared by motion and existing things more generally.
That is, the reasoning and learning that depend on basic concepts. A concept is not acquired through a judgment; definitions and proofs share basic concepts.

The author points out that our direct awareness that something exists, and our grasp of simple affirmative statements, help us form these ideas immediately. Their precise definitions may still require reasoning. The question here is whether we grasp their nature directly, not whether we immediately know that they exist.

Motion is a kind of waiting and striving. Any part of motion is likewise waiting and striving: it is neither pure actuality nor pure potentiality, nor is it complete all at once like a square when the square shape is attained.

“With” here means that the potentiality is bound up with actuality. Motion lies between pure potentiality and complete actuality. It does not mean the pure potentiality that precedes every actuality; otherwise, every event preceded by potentiality would count as motion, even if the potentiality were not itself actual in any way.

A completion removes some lack. Motion removes a particular potentiality, so it completes a thing only in the respect in which it was potential. It does not complete the body simply as a body. The body’s first completion as a body is its specific form. It is mistaken to say that this definition is harder to understand than motion itself. We may know that something has come to be before we understand its nature; what is hard to grasp is that its coming-to-be is continuous, from one stable state to another, without a pause.

The note suggests that “otherness” may not have been intended as a strict definition, but as a change of wording, like explaining a natural kind as a universal concept or as a particular determination. If the definition may use a broader term, “striving” or “desire” would be more fitting than “otherness.” Out of respect for his teachers, however, Pythagoras may have chosen the latter. Another possible reading is that motion is what makes the natural world different from the divine realm: the latter has no waiting or change. Motion is what makes these two domains distinct.
The two expressions may have had a special technical sense among those philosophers, referring to continuous change rather than their ordinary or general meanings.

Motion itself is a source of many apparent contradictions, like a difficult passage of scripture. If we say it exists, we are right; if we say it does not, we are also right, because it is potentiality and potentiality is not a thing, even though it is actual in one respect. If we call motion one, we are right, because its continuous unity makes it one thing. If we call it many, we are right, because it can be divided without limit. It is both changing and, in the sense of being between its endpoints, stable.

This challenges the claim that motion is unlimited. It is one continuous, particular thing. It is unlimited only in the imagined divisions of its magnitude, which is time or something that matches time. Straight-line motion is unlimited only in thought.
I say: granted that motion is change, it is not the same as otherness or difference.
“Nature” here means the source of a thing’s own motion and rest. The word can also mean a general essence.

Gradual change occurs in the external world even in motion understood as “being between,” as the phrase “even in the imagination” suggests. Being at one point in the middle is simple. If a distance were made of indivisible points, passing through each one would not be gradual. But measured against the continuous boundaries of the distance, the body’s being between points is gradual. Though simple, it flows like a moving instant.

This is essential to the answer: motion can be said to exist, but its existence is intertwined with nonexistence, because it has no indivisible part. Matter is actual only as potentiality; the two are intertwined there too.
Instability belongs to the meanings of these three categories—when, action, and being acted on—quite apart from whether they exist.

“Immaterial souls” means souls considered apart from the body. Their stable states include universal acts of will and intellectual ideas in themselves. These are not motions. If thought is called motion, as when people speak of reasoning from a question to first principles and back to a conclusion, then “motion” is being used broadly for transition. Imaginative souls also undergo changes in particular acts of will and perception. These changes are tied to the body, since such souls depend strongly on it; Avicenna holds that particular powers are embedded in the subtle bodily spirit.

Motion is also a completion and actuality, while leaving a state is removal or absence. The idea of continuous gradual change may be understood in “passing” or “leaving a state.” The phrase may also derive from “engaging in” or “practising,” in which case the objection to the definition would not apply.

“Reaching” means reaching essentially, not merely encountering things that happen to lie along the way. The moving thing is left unspecified so that the definition includes both bodies and matter, as in substantial motion, as well as motion in quantity. “Gradual” is already implied by calling the boundaries potential: each boundary is a state of waiting that leads to another. “Continuously” is not redundant. A movement could proceed through separate intervals divided by rests; both the potential boundaries and their continuity are needed. This definition makes continuous gradual change clearer than the alternatives.

Imagining boundaries, or saying that a body lies between the starting point and the destination, is only a way of indicating the particular state involved in motion. But introducing those boundaries also allows us to divide motion into parts. Divisibility belongs to motion as a continuous course, not to the simple state of being between its endpoints.

Existing things fall into two groups: things whose own existence is what we point to, and things that exist because something real gives the mind grounds to derive them. Relations and motion as a continuous whole belong to the second group. If a relation existed in itself, it would have to be an accident, like whiteness, and itself have a relation of inherence to its subject. That would lead to an endless chain. Nor is it merely imaginary, since it exists as long as its real basis exists.

Time, like motion, has two senses. Time that matches motion as a continuous whole exists only in the mind. Time that matches motion as “being between” is the flowing instant, and exists along with that motion. Avicenna’s claim that time exists outside the mind refers to the second sense. The past and future do not exist, whether they are long stretches or what we ordinarily call the present. Only the flowing state and the flowing instant—the core of time—exist. Time as the measure of a continuous whole exists through its real basis, which lets us divide it into hours and days. What we sense and imagine is often confused with what exists outside us.

On this account, motion can be considered as arising all at once: this is motion as “being between.” Or it can be considered as arising gradually: this is motion as a continuous whole. In the second case, if its gradual arising and passing away are both considered, it exists outside the mind; if its continuing existence is considered as complete all at once, it exists only in the mind.

There is no contradiction. Time as the flowing instant exists, so motion as “being between,” which it contains, also exists. Time as the measure of the continuous whole and motion as a continuous whole exist only through their real basis.

The objection accepts that “being between” is vague and tries to offset that vagueness with particular features. One could say these pull in opposite directions and cancel out. Better to say that the vagueness is a mistake caused by confusing what is in the mind with what exists outside it. Universality belongs to the general idea in the mind. What exists outside the mind is an expansive, particular motion, not a universal concept or a randomly chosen instance. It is like the “some form” that makes matter receptive to a bodily form: what is meant is not the general idea or a single instance, but a broad reality that applies to a continuous series of particular forms.

For these philosophers, motion is not made particular by the unity of one specific mover. It remains one even when several things successively draw or push it along, as with motion in place, or several sources of heat, as with change in quality.

Strictly speaking, the answer accepts a connection between what exists and what does not exist—but this kind of nonexistence is not sheer nothingness. Motion is actual in one respect: its subject is at the starting point. In another respect, the continuous passage toward the destination is still potential, because motion is always passing away. In these weak kinds of existence, it is possible for actuality and this kind of nonexistence to be connected. The same holds for time, which measures motion.

A thing’s state can be divided into parts, some actual in relation to others and still potential in relation to what comes later. If we imagine a quality divided into three parts, for instance, the second is actual relative to the first and potential relative to the third. Further division does not change this. The parts exist only potentially, so existence is intertwined with nonexistence, actuality with potentiality, and coming to be with passing away. Each part requires the passing away of another; it is itself the passing away of what came before. The actuality of a later part begins only when the potentiality for it gives way.

Calling motion an “action” seems to prepare for the first argument below: motion is an action in relation to its mover and something undergone in relation to what is moved. If mover and moved were the same, acting and being acted on would be one category, which is impossible. But it is not clear that this distinction follows from the definition of motion already given. Motion is not itself in one of the categories, and neither are moving and being moved, which are ways of relating to motion. This point is sound for heating and being heated, which are action and undergoing, while heat belongs to the category of quality.
Motion is made up of potentiality intertwined with actuality, just as prime matter is pure potentiality and is what makes a body a substance that is only potentially actual.

Manuscripts differ here. Some read “the mover,” and in the example “the heater,” where the intended reading is “the moving thing” and “the thing being heated.” That version is poor in meaning: the point is that a moving thing needs a mover, not that a mover must itself have something moved by it. The grammar also supports the standard reading. In the next clause, the pronoun refers to what is being heated, not the heater.

Nature contains, in an integrated way, the effects that gradually appear in matter. The nature of fire, for example, contains the different instances of heat that flow from it. Likewise, the rational soul’s active power gathers the different kinds of knowledge and will that come from it. In its own self-subsisting existence, the soul is knowledge and will.
In their account, substance is stable.

In their account, the mover is not itself subject to the possibility of motion. Some copies read “in itself,” meaning its essence, which is possible; on that reading, “not potential” means it is not like an essence or prime matter. The claim that motion is not a completion of what is already actual explains the previous point.

This point is clear if we accept that a direct mover is not actual in motion itself, as do those who deny substantial motion. But for us, natures flow and change. Here “motion” means the accidental motion in the four categories; “something other than motion” means nature, and “by necessity” means that this motion follows from it.

If each motion were caused by another motion in an accidental category, the chain would have to end in motion belonging to something substantial. A merely conceptual change, such as growing nearer to a natural place, is not enough. The details will follow.

It has also been established that motion always lies between two endpoints: one free from the potentiality and possibility involved in motion, the other potential in relation to all the actual states along the way. It has also been established that a body whose substance moves is made of matter and form, joined as one.

Prime matter also has goodness in itself, since it exists, and everything that exists is either purely good or has more good than evil. The potentiality for existence is also a kind of existence, and a shadow is a kind of light when compared with darkness. The author explicitly distinguishes matter from absolute nonexistence. The point is clearer still if matter and form are understood as joined together.

The argument is that the subject of motion disappears. Motion is defined as a completion that follows potentiality. If a body moved itself, and what belongs to it by nature could never be absent from it, there would be no prior potentiality for motion in it. Motion would be actual in the body, even though motion is a first completion and must raise some potentiality.

There is another possibility: bodily form may mean a substance that can receive dimensions. On that meaning, it is the feature that divides substance into kinds and makes bodyhood what it is. It is still one and the same nature, and bodyhood is one kind.

“Self-evident” does not mean that the claim needs no explanation for anyone. The comparison with self-evident truths is not inconsistent with the philosophers proving it elsewhere. Some minds need a reminder; the point itself takes reasoning to establish. They mean by bodyhood a thing that can receive three dimensions—three lines crossing at right angles. What makes it receptive is extension. If that feature differed by kind, the difference would have to be between heavenly, elemental, fiery, or airy bodies, but such differences do not explain what makes all of them receptive to dimensions. A difference in the essence of what receives them is also impossible if they all share that capacity. No feature other than extension—even a single indivisible substance or a collection of them—can explain that capacity. As Avicenna says, a body is continuous by its very nature; if it were divided, it would not cease to be able to receive dimensions. Al-Razi’s objection is therefore unsound.
The same answer applies to the fifth and sixth arguments. The same point also applies to some arguments against treating different kinds of matter as sources of different motions.
That is, they differ as heavenly bodies or as bodies made of the elements, and elemental bodies differ from one another accordingly. The same applies to the claim that bodies have different natures.
“A feature present in bodyhood” could mean nature, or some other feature.

The objection treats the general kind in a mental combination and matter—the extended prime matter—in a physical compound as if each existed independently, with form added later. It then asks what makes the body acquire its special effects, whether bodyhood or something else. But the general kind and matter are not independent things in the external world that receive their form or special effects afterward. Form and the feature that makes a kind particular are what make the general kind and matter actual. The former are indeterminate; form and species make them determinate. Bodyhood is a general feature of particular natures, not the other way around. See the discussion of how a defining feature makes a general kind a particular kind.

Once al-Razi grants that one thing cannot be both agent and recipient, his claim that essences produce and receive their necessary features contradicts that admission. One might interpret his “strongest objection” as a counterargument rather than an objection from within his own argument, and read “disproves” in the looser sense of “challenges.” Even then, the problem remains.

“By itself” is the opposite of “incidentally.” Avicenna’s discussion in the last part of The Healing divides movers into those that move incidentally and those that move in themselves. A mover may move incidentally in itself—for example, any power in a body moves along with the body—or incidentally through something else, as wind moves a person sitting in a boat when it moves the boat. A mover that acts in itself may act directly, or through one or more intermediaries. An intermediary connected to the mover, such as a hand, is called an instrument; one separate from it, such as an axe, is called a tool. Some authors do not distinguish these terms.

This proof is based on Avicenna’s argument from the middle term and the endpoints, which he uses to show that a causal chain cannot continue without end. It establishes that motions must ultimately come from an intellective mover that does not itself move by its own nature.

The alternatives include the three intellectual powers of the theoretical mind, the acquired intellect, and the particular powers of the animal soul. If the separate being's power is a particular power that perceives, it still does not explain why it affects this body rather than another; its relation to all bodies would be the same. There is another possibility: the separate being acts by its own nature. The author does not discuss it here, perhaps because it is plainly unable to act directly on a particular body. The phrase “particular motions” points to this: how could a separate being directly bring about a specific motion if its relation to all bodies were equal?
The argument is adapted from Avicenna, with a small change in how it is stated.

One might object that denying that a thing is impossible or already necessary gives us only its possibility in itself. Its nature could carry this possibility, so matter would not be needed. The reply is that matter is needed because this thing comes after another thing in time, not merely because it is neither impossible nor necessary. A nature does not exist earlier in time than the thing itself.

Otherwise, the thing would have to come before itself. An agent's ability to bring something about depends on the possibility of its effect, since no one can bring about what is impossible. This argument tries to avoid the need for prior matter by saying that the effect only needs an agent, not a subject. The reply is that possibility belongs to the thing affected, while ability belongs to the agent. It is like defining God's ability by saying that He can do what is possible: the possibility is on the side of what is made, not a feature that defines the agent.
Unlike possibility in itself, which consists of two negations and is purely negative, readiness is a real feature of a subject. It is not an abstract idea of a thing's nature.
Readiness can be stronger or weaker as a possible thing comes closer to or farther from being actual. Such degrees belong to realities outside the mind, not to abstract ideas.

“What is ready” is the particular thing it is ready to become. In this sense, readiness is a possibility for a specific result. Considered as a feature of the matter or subject itself, it is called a disposition or capacity, rather than possibility.
“Existence in general” means existence as a simple fact, as in “something exists.” “Limited existence” means existence with a feature, as in “Zayd is writing.”

If readiness were a settled quality, then it would itself be something that could exist or fail to exist; it would be possible, rather than possibility. The comparison with a self-standing thing is not meant to say that it exists without a subject. The point is that readiness is a relation, not a separate settled feature. Readiness is the basis for the possibility of something that can follow it, not the same thing as the readiness itself. It is a real relation to what may come to be, and so a relation in the full sense. A settled quality is called an “accident” in the traditional classification; a relation is not a settled quality in that sense.
The possibility of becoming something is the relation itself, distinct from the underlying readiness. “In general” includes the soul, qualities, and forms.
This note clarifies the grammar: “rather” refers to the phrase immediately before it.

Readiness is a state in a subject that connects it to a possible thing. When the mind considers it, it sees a relation with two sides: the subject's potential to become that thing, and the thing's potential to exist in that subject.

Calling this readiness “potential existence,” as opposed to actual existence, is a way of speaking. The division of existence into actual and potential means that something either exists independently, without being related to another thing, or is a real capacity for something that can exist in a subject. The latter is still a kind of existence.

Matter must also remain through changes. It lets us say that what comes to be is the same thing that passed away, since one form does not turn into another and the forms are different. If matter did not remain, we could not call the new thing a change of the old one. One might reply that an endless series of matters is not impossible if each is only earlier in time than the next. But readiness for existence exists in the same subject as the thing that is coming to be.
This points ahead to substantial motion: matter and form are joined as one, and matter follows the form as both are renewed.

The problem is not simply that a relation is repeated in the mind. The deeper question is how a real relation can connect something that exists with something that does not yet exist, since a relation itself must exist and needs both sides to be present in the same realm. The answer is that the readiness for a coming form is a real feature of a subject, but the subject is not the first form that will pass away. It is an underlying substance that continues through the change. The new form is not yet present with all its effects, but it has a weaker kind of existence in the subject as the form that is about to come to be. Once it becomes fully actual, its readiness ends—not because one thing vanished and another unrelated thing appeared, but because the same underlying matter took on the new form.

The same is true of all changes in time: something changes into something else, whether a form or a quality, as when air becomes fire or water, or a body takes on a new quality or size. The matter holds the readiness for what can come next. Because the matter remains, the earlier thing and the later thing are connected. It can hold the potentiality for all forms, and the forms appear one after another in continuous change. Each form is actual in its own time and potential before that. The earlier form and its potentiality for the next one belong to one continuous, changing existence. Matter is joined to form, not simply added beside it.

This is substantial motion: matter itself moves through forms. What exists in potential is a real, weaker level of existence, without all the effects of what exists fully in actuality. This explains how we can divide all existence into what is actual and what is potential, and how matter and form are joined as one. Many further results follow, which the author will explain where they belong.

The point of the condition is that two positive, existing things can still be potentiality. The thing that can come to be is particular, such as water. Pure potentiality means the capacity for existence in general, as in an essence considered apart from whether it exists.

The earlier argument applies to human souls that are connected to matter as something they govern, even if they are not embedded in it like bodily forms. This follows the view held by Aristotle’s followers that the human soul is separate from matter from its first moment. On Mulla Sadra's view that the soul begins bodily and later becomes spiritual, the point is clearer still. The argument also applies to nonhuman souls, whether one thinks they are material or separate, and to bodily qualities.
Matter does not come before a general kind in time. Nor does a general kind, simply as a body, cause particular motions. It is the particular body and its particular nature that cause them.

If these thinkers meant that matter came first in time—whether they called it matter, darkness, an abyss, or an empty space—their view is false. It assumes matter existed without any form, as though God had stopped giving existence. It also implies that light came after darkness, and leads to other problems. If they meant that matter comes first in the order of being, that too is backwards: a general kind becomes a particular kind through its form, and matter becomes actual through form. If they meant a place in the order of ideas, there is no problem, provided prime matter is treated as the lowest starting point in a rise through more complete forms, toward the greatest light. Some old accounts describe the world as first dark and empty, then filled with plants and animals, then with spirits and human beings. This can be understood as a sequence of increasing order and completeness.

The author mentions this view here even though its usual form seems to deny potentiality and change: everything is said to exist already, with some things hidden and others appearing as order comes about.

Taken literally, this supports the view that potentiality is a weaker level of actuality, which does not yet have all the effects of full actuality. Otherwise, it makes no sense to say that a substantial form completes a readiness in matter if that readiness disappears as soon as the new form arrives.

The wording should be “and existence,” with “and” understood. The point is that potentiality is not nothing; it has a kind of existence. Existence comes before an essence in reality, and potentiality is one such essence whose existence is actual.

This follows from the meaning of Avicenna's words. In a particular case, one capacity may come before a particular act in time, but another act comes before that capacity. More broadly, actuality comes before potentiality. The claim that actuality comes first in time is part of the general point; the later arguments explain the other kinds of priority.

One might say that matter is the subject of substantial motion, or even of motion in quantity. The reply is that the previous argument follows the philosophers' view that matter with a particular form is the subject of a particular change. In the same way, matter with a particular size moves through changes in quantity.

The body does exist outside the mind, but in particular kinds; it does not exist as an undefined body on a level with those kinds. The second argument is that if motion were a form that divided bodies into kinds, it would have to complete an undefined body. But no such body exists outside the mind. So a particular body must already exist before motion affects it.

This repeats the first point: an accident cannot make a substance into a particular kind. The third argument also rests on the principle that what is merely potential cannot give a kind to something already actual.

This argument assumes that motion as a continuous whole exists outside the mind. If we deny that, we could object that what exists outside is motion as “being between,” which is stable enough to belong to a stable subject. This resembles arguments about how a changing thing can be connected to an eternal cause.

The renewal of nature's existence is an essential feature, not a later addition. This is what the author means by saying that the immediate mover's existence includes motion. The pronoun in “its immediate mover” refers to accidental motion, which is a later feature of its subject; the wording shifts between these senses. Substantial motion belongs to nature itself and is not separately caused. The author says no act of making comes between nature's existence and this necessary feature.
